name: What are awk and sed?
description:
Text Processing Powertools

awk and sed are command-line tools for processing and transforming text. They're essential for any Linux user.

  • sed — Stream Editor. Best for find-and-replace, deleting lines, inserting text.
  • awk — Pattern scanning and processing. Best for extracting columns, calculations, formatted output.

First, let's create a sample file to work with:

$ cat > /tmp/employees.txt << 'EOF'
John Sales 5000
Jane Engineering 7500
Bob Sales 4500
Alice Engineering 8000
Charlie Marketing 5500
Diana Marketing 6000
EOF

Verify:

$ cat /tmp/employees.txt

name: sed: Find and Replace
description:
sed Substitution

The most common sed operation — find and replace:

$ sed 's/Sales/Business/' /tmp/employees.txt

This replaces the first occurrence on each line. To replace all occurrences, add g:

$ sed 's/Sales/Business/g' /tmp/employees.txt

Note: this prints the result but doesn't modify the file. To edit in-place, use -i:

$ sed -i 's/Sales/Business/g' /tmp/employees.txt
$ cat /tmp/employees.txt

Case-insensitive replacement with I flag:

$ sed 's/engineering/ENGINEERING/Ig' /tmp/employees.txt

Let's restore our test data for the next steps:

$ cat > /tmp/employees.txt << 'EOF'
John Sales 5000
Jane Engineering 7500
Bob Sales 4500
Alice Engineering 8000
Charlie Marketing 5500
Diana Marketing 6000
EOF

name: sed: Print and Delete Lines
description:
Line Operations with sed

Print specific lines (use -n to suppress default output and p to print):

# Print line 3 only
$ sed -n '3p' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print lines 2 to 4
$ sed -n '2,4p' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print last line
$ sed -n '$p' /tmp/employees.txt

Delete lines with d:

# Delete line 1
$ sed '1d' /tmp/employees.txt

# Delete last line
$ sed '$d' /tmp/employees.txt

# Delete lines containing 'Sales'
$ sed '/Sales/d' /tmp/employees.txt

Print lines matching a pattern:

$ sed -n '/Engineering/p' /tmp/employees.txt

name: sed: Insert and Append
description:
Adding Text with sed

Insert a line before line 3:

$ sed '3i\New line inserted here' /tmp/employees.txt

Append a line after line 3:

$ sed '3a\New line appended here' /tmp/employees.txt

Add a header at the beginning:

$ sed '1i\Name Department Salary' /tmp/employees.txt

Add a footer at the end:

$ sed '$a\--- End of Report ---' /tmp/employees.txt

Replace an entire line:

# Replace line 2 entirely
$ sed '2c\Jane Engineering 9000' /tmp/employees.txt

name: awk: Print Columns
description:
awk Column Extraction

awk splits each line into fields. By default, fields are separated by whitespace.

# Print the first column (names)
$ awk '{print $1}' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print column 1 and 3 (name and salary)
$ awk '{print $1, $3}' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print with custom format
$ awk '{print $1 " earns $" $3}' /tmp/employees.txt

Special variables:

  • $0 — the entire line
  • $1, $2, $3... — individual fields
  • NF — number of fields
  • NR — current line number
# Print line numbers with content
$ awk '{print NR, $0}' /tmp/employees.txt

name: awk: Pattern Matching
description:
Filtering with awk

awk can filter lines based on conditions:

# Print only Engineering employees
$ awk '$2 == "Engineering"' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print employees earning more than 5500
$ awk '$3 > 5500' /tmp/employees.txt

# Print names of Sales employees
$ awk '$2 == "Sales" {print $1}' /tmp/employees.txt

Pattern matching with regex:

# Lines containing 'Mar'
$ awk '/Mar/' /tmp/employees.txt

# Lines NOT containing 'Sales'
$ awk '!/Sales/' /tmp/employees.txt

Combine conditions:

# Engineering AND salary > 7000
$ awk '$2 == "Engineering" && $3 > 7000' /tmp/employees.txt

name: awk: Calculations
description:
Math with awk

awk can do calculations — great for reports.

Sum all salaries:

$ awk '{sum += $3} END {print "Total:", sum}' /tmp/employees.txt

Average salary:

$ awk '{sum += $3; count++} END {print "Average:", sum/count}' /tmp/employees.txt

Sum by department:

$ awk '{dept[$2] += $3} END {for (d in dept) print d, dept[d]}' /tmp/employees.txt

Find the highest salary:

$ awk 'BEGIN {max=0} $3>max {max=$3; name=$1} END {print name, max}' /tmp/employees.txt

This is where awk really shines — quick data analysis without needing Python or a spreadsheet.
answer: The BEGIN block runs before processing any lines. The END block runs after all lines are processed. The middle block runs for each line.

name: awk: Custom Separators and Formatting
description:
Advanced awk

Use a different field separator with -F. Create a CSV file:

$ cat > /tmp/data.csv << 'EOF'
John,Sales,5000
Jane,Engineering,7500
Bob,Sales,4500
EOF

Parse CSV:

$ awk -F',' '{print $1, $3}' /tmp/data.csv

Formatted output with printf:

$ awk -F',' '{printf "%-10s %-15s $%d\n", $1, $2, $3}' /tmp/data.csv

Output:

John       Sales           $5000
Jane       Engineering     $7500
Bob        Sales           $4500

Combine sed and awk in a pipeline:

# Remove header, extract names of high earners
$ sed '1d' /tmp/employees.txt | awk '$3 > 5000 {print $1}'

These tools are the building blocks of shell scripting. Master them and you can process any text file.
